title: US Visa Fraud Crackdown Widens: Nine Universities Probed Over J-1, Outsourcers Suspended
excerpt: Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito's campaign now spans an H-1B criminal probe, J-1 subpoenas to Harvard, MIT and seven other universities, PERM suspensions for Microsoft, Adobe and six IT outsourcers, and a new Visa Fraud Strike Team.
body:
• The Trump administration's visa-fraud crackdown has widened from warnings to machinery: a multi-agency Visa Fraud Strike Team, subpoenas to nine major universities over J-1 use, and PERM suspensions for Microsoft, Adobe and six large IT outsourcers.
  • Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito says investigators have issued dozens of subpoenas in an H-1B probe covering alleged fake employers, sham jobs and wage kickbacks — "we have handcuffs ready."
  • At the nine universities, the administration says foreign nationals hold about 61% of federally funded postdoc and researcher roles, versus 38% elsewhere; the universities say every J-1 holder was vetted and authorised by the US government.
  • For Indians — 71% of approved H-1B beneficiaries in FY2024 — nothing here changes a rule, a cap or a fee. It changes the enforcement climate every petition, LCA and consular interview now sits in.

The warning the Hindustan Times summarised this week — that H-1B and J-1 visa fraud threatens American jobs and security — is no longer just rhetoric. Over the past month the Trump administration has built an enforcement campaign around it: a criminal H-1B investigation led by the Labor Department's inspector general, subpoenas to nine of America's most prestigious universities over their use of J-1 exchange visas, the suspension of Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT outsourcing firms from the permanent labour certification (PERM) programme, and a new multi-agency Visa Fraud Strike Team.

"Subpoenas have been served. Investigations are underway. And nobody gets a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building."

— Anthony P. D'Esposito, Inspector General, US Department of Labor

The University Probe

On October 9, at a White House Fraud Task Force event with Vice President JD Vance, Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced that subpoenas had been served on nine universities — Harvard, MIT, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech and Arizona State — over alleged misuse of J-1 classifications in federally funded research. The administration says foreign nationals hold roughly 61 percent of postdoctoral and researcher positions supported by federal grants at those institutions, against 38 percent at other universities, and is examining whether the J-1 route was used to avoid employment obligations and undercut American researchers. Vance put it bluntly: the universities are "using these visas way too much... to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers."

The universities reject any suggestion of wrongdoing. MIT noted that each of its J-1 holders "has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government"; Stanford and Yale said they comply with all visa laws and will cooperate. A subpoena begins an investigation — it does not establish a violation.

The Employer Side: PERM Suspensions and an H-1B Probe

A day earlier, on October 8, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling suspended Microsoft and Adobe — and, with them, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini — from the PERM programme, meaning no new or pending permanent labour certifications will be processed for those firms while federal investigations run. D'Esposito's office is separately running a criminal investigation into alleged foreign-labour fraud — fake employers, sham jobs, "visa mills," wage kickbacks — and says dozens of subpoenas and search warrants have already been executed. On X, he has warned that "a secure border means locking every door, including the H-1B back door," and that the foreign labour programme "is going to look very different 365 days from now."

The legal spine is a September 18 executive order on H-1B programme integrity, which asserts a wage gap of $9,000 to $20,000 between H-1B holders and comparable US-born workers, directs agencies to weigh whether a sponsoring employer has recently laid off similarly situated Americans, and orders a review of previously filed labour condition applications. The $100,000 payment required for many H-1B petitions from outside the US has been extended through September 21, 2027.

What It Means for Indian Professionals

India-born beneficiaries accounted for 283,397 — about 71 percent — of approved H-1B beneficiaries in FY2024, and Indian physicians and researchers are a large presence in J-1 programmes. None of this week's machinery changes eligibility for either visa. What it changes is scrutiny: employers under investigation face frozen green-card pipelines for their staff, universities face document demands, and individual applicants should expect fraud-focused verification of jobs, worksites and wages. Microsoft, for its part, says about 80 percent of its recent H-1B filings extended or changed the status of existing employees rather than adding new hires. The investigations will now test both sides' claims — in files, not posts.

Editor's note: an earlier version of this article centred on a social-media post that could not be independently verified on review. It has been rewritten around the documented enforcement actions above.
nri_angle: Indians are 71% of H-1B beneficiaries and a large share of J-1 researchers and physicians; the crackdown changes the enforcement climate — frozen PERM pipelines at major employers, fraud-focused scrutiny — without changing any visa rule itself.
author: Diaspora Desk
